lead: Every celestial fix is a time fix: four seconds of error are a mile of longitude. Three clocks run on an ocean passage, UT, ship's time and local mean time; always know which one you hold.

qa.q: How do I convert longitude into time to get UT from local mean time?
qa.a: At 15° to the hour: 1° is 4 minutes, 1′ is 4 seconds. Then UT is **local mean time** plus west longitude in time, or minus east longitude in time.

blocks.p: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so longitude and time are one thing in two units. **Local mean time** (LMT) is mean time on your meridian; **UT** is LMT at Greenwich.

blocks.rule: UT = LMT + west longitude in time, or − east longitude in time.

blocks.p: The **equation of time** is the gap between the true Sun and the mean Sun, up to about 16 minutes. You never apply it yourself: the almanac's Mer Pass, 1144 LMT in early November, 1214 in February, is noon with it already in. Apply your longitude in time for the UT of local noon; timing the Sun at its highest and comparing with Mer Pass gives your longitude.

sections.title: The clock the crew lives by

qa.q: How do I convert ship's time to UT using the zone description?
qa.a: Add the **zone description**: UT = zone time + ZD, where ZD is the longitude divided by 15 and rounded, positive west and negative east. Ship's time 1530 with ZD +4 is 1930 UT.

refs: Time — shore time and ship's time
Time — ship's time and the watch rota

blocks.p: The world is cut into 24 **zones** 15° wide, centred on 0°, 15°, 30° and so on, with boundaries at 7°30′, 22°30′, 37°30′ … The **zone description** (ZD) is the longitude divided by 15 and rounded, positive west and negative east.

blocks.rule: UT = zone time + ZD. Ship's time 1530, ZD +4: 1930 UT.

fig.note: Westbound: clocks back an hour at each boundary

blocks.p: Keep the ship's clocks on the zone you are in: westbound retard them an hour at each boundary, eastbound advance them. A retarded night makes one watch five hours long, so split the hour among the night watches. Shore time is whatever the country keeps, summer time and half-hour zones included. Log sights, fixes and radio schedules in UT, which never jumps.

qa.q: Do I gain or lose a day crossing the date line westbound?
qa.a: You skip a day: crossing the **date line** westbound into east longitude, the date goes forward; eastbound you repeat one. Hours and minutes do not change, and UT and its date run on.

blocks.p: East of 180° the zone is ZD +12, west of it ZD −12: the same clock time, a day apart. Crossing westbound into east longitude you skip a day, the date goes forward; eastbound you repeat one. Hours and minutes do not change.

fig.note: Westbound across the date line: the date goes forward

blocks.p: The deck watch on UT is not touched: **UT and its date run on**, and they are what the almanac wants. Convert first and open the Greenwich date, which may differ from the ship's: at 0745 on 15 March with ZD −12 the sight is at 1945 UT on 14 March. A passage time is the difference of the two UTs, not of the local dates.

qa.q: How do I work out my deck watch error from its daily rate?
qa.a: Error now = last error + **rate** × days, the rate being how the error changes each day. A watch 18 s fast and gaining 2 s a day is 28 s fast five days later.

blocks.p: A watch is never right; it is **fast** or **slow** by a known error, and the **rate** is how that error changes each day: error now = last error + rate × days. Heat alters the rate, so in the tropics use the rate from recent checks, not the one from Biscay.

blocks.p: Check against a radio time signal, WWV or the hourly pips, the hour being the start of the long pip; UTC is UT within a second, and the signal's travel time is nothing. Set the watch from a GPS only on its UTC display: raw GPS time runs 18 seconds ahead. Carry two or three watches and compare them daily: one that jumps shows against the others.

blocks.p: A minute of longitude is a mile only on the equator: multiply by the cosine of the latitude. Time a sight with a stopwatch started at the instant and read against the watch after; a timekeeper notes the seconds first.

sections.title: From UT to GHA and declination

qa.q: How do I get the Sun's GHA for a sight taken between whole hours?
qa.a: Take the GHA for the whole hour of UT from the **daily pages**, by Greenwich date, then add the increment for the minutes and seconds from the increments table; correct Dec by d's share.

blocks.p: The **daily pages** give GHA and Dec for every whole hour of UT, by Greenwich date. The **increments** table adds the minutes and seconds, with columns for the Sun and planets at 15° an hour, Aries at 15°02.5′ and the Moon. The Dec changes by d an hour; for the minutes add or subtract d's share, the sign by inspection of the next hour.

fig.title: GHA and Dec for a sight

blocks.p: The last second of an hour belongs to that hour's row, with 59 m 59 s of increment. A watch on ship's time is first turned into UT with its date: a sight at midnight can belong to tomorrow's page.

sections.title: The almanac's times are LMT

qa.q: Are the almanac's sunrise, sunset and twilight times in UT or local time?
qa.a: In **LMT**, against latitude: interpolate for yours, add west longitude in time or subtract east for UT, then take off the ZD for ship's time.

refs: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT
Time — planets' and stars' meridian passage

blocks.p: Sunrise, sunset, twilight and meridian passage are tabulated in **LMT** against latitude: interpolate for yours, add west longitude in time (subtract east) for UT, then take off the ZD for ship's time. Shortcut: ship's time is the LMT plus 4 minutes for every degree you are west of the zone's central meridian.

fig.title: Sunset by ship's time
lines: Long in time 3 h 20 min: 2120 UT

blocks.p: Star sights live between **civil twilight**, Sun 6° down, and **nautical twilight**, 12° down: horizon and stars together. In high-latitude summer the almanac prints //// where the Sun never gets that low: plan on sun lines. The Moon crosses the meridian about 50 minutes later each day: interpolate between the two days' values by longitude, west longitude towards the next day. A planet with Mer Pass near noon is lost in the Sun; one in the evening or early morning gives a twilight sight.
